items.stem: Briefly explain why the Treaty of Versailles provided Hitler with opportunities for expansion.
items.answer: Its territorial losses (Polish Corridor, Saar, Sudeten Germans outside the Reich) and military restrictions were widely resented, so revision commanded broad German support; and its creation of small successor states in Eastern Europe left a power vacuum.

items.stem: Distinguish between the intentionalist interpretation of Hitler’s foreign policy and the structuralist interpretation.
items.answer: Intentionalists (e.g. Trevor-Roper, Hildebrand) argue Hitler followed a long-held programme from Mein Kampf; structuralists/functionalists (e.g. Mommsen, Broszat) and A. J. P. Taylor stress opportunism, economic pressures and the dynamics of the Nazi state. Many historians combine fixed aims with opportunist methods.

Source D
The acquisition of new soil for the settlement of our surplus population has an infinite number of advantages. But such a territorial policy cannot be carried out in the Cameroons; it can be carried out almost exclusively in Europe. If we speak of soil in Europe today, we can primarily have in mind only Russia and her vassal border states.
— Adolf Hitler, Mein Kampf, volume 2, written 1925–1926 (adapted translation)

items.answer: Germany needed new land for settlement; colonies overseas were not the solution; Lebensraum must be found in Europe, chiefly at the expense of Russia and its border states.

items.stem:
Source A
Hitler’s foreign policy was that of his predecessors, of the professional diplomats at the foreign ministry, and indeed of virtually all Germans. He wished to free Germany from the restrictions of the peace treaty. In principle and doctrine, Hitler was no more wicked than many other contemporary statesmen.
— A. J. P. Taylor, British historian, The Origins of the Second World War (1961) (paraphrased)

Limitations: Taylor wrote before many archives were available and deliberately provocative; he has been criticised for underplaying Nazi ideology and the Hossbach evidence.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "autarky"?
options: “living space”: Hitler’s aim, set out in Mein Kampf, of acquiring territory in Eastern Europe for German settlement at the expense of the Slavic peoples
The April 1935 agreement of Britain, France and Italy to resist German violations of Versailles, which collapsed over Abyssinia
The status Mussolini adopted in September 1939: siding politically with Germany but not entering the war
Economic self-sufficiency, pursued by Nazi Germany (Four-Year Plan, 1936) and Fascist Italy (the “Battle for Grain”) to prepare for war
items.answer: Economic self-sufficiency, pursued by Nazi Germany (Four-Year Plan, 1936) and Fascist Italy (the “Battle for Grain”) to prepare for war
items.markingKey: D. "autarky" is economic self-sufficiency, pursued by Nazi Germany (Four-Year Plan, 1936) and Fascist Italy (the “Battle for Grain”) to prepare for war.

items.stem: Priya writes: "Mussolini’s foreign policy was consistently aggressive from 1922." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: In the 1920s Mussolini mostly cooperated with Britain and France (Locarno 1925, Kellogg–Briand 1928) despite Corfu (1923); he even opposed Hitler over Austria in 1934 and joined the Stresa Front in 1935.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Sudetenland"?
options: The border regions of Czechoslovakia with a German-speaking majority of about three million, claimed by Hitler in 1938
The union of Austria with Germany, prohibited by the Treaty of Versailles and carried out by German occupation on 12–13 March 1938
The status Mussolini adopted in September 1939: siding politically with Germany but not entering the war
“our sea”: Mussolini’s ambition to make the Mediterranean an Italian-dominated sea, reviving the Roman Empire
items.answer: The border regions of Czechoslovakia with a German-speaking majority of about three million, claimed by Hitler in 1938
items.markingKey: A. "Sudetenland" is the border regions of Czechoslovakia with a German-speaking majority of about three million, claimed by Hitler in 1938.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Austria was annexed in March 1938 rather than earlier.
items.answer: In 1934 Mussolini had moved troops to the Brenner to stop a Nazi coup; by 1938 the Rome–Berlin Axis meant Italy acquiesced, and when Schuschnigg called a plebiscite on independence Hitler forced his resignation and sent in troops.

items.stem: Distinguish between the “guilty men” view of appeasement and the revisionist view of appeasement.
items.answer: The “guilty men” view (Cato, 1940) condemned Chamberlain for weakness and naivety; revisionists such as Donald Cameron Watt and John Charmley argued appeasement was a rational response to military, economic and imperial constraints; counter-revisionists (R. A. C. Parker) argue alternatives such as an alliance with the USSR were available.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Munich Agreement (September 1938) shows appeasement as a policy of concession to avoid war.
items.answer: Chamberlain, Daladier, Hitler and Mussolini agreed that Germany would occupy the Sudetenland in stages from 1 October; Chamberlain returned with a signed Anglo-German declaration, claiming “peace for our time”. Britain and France sacrificed Czechoslovakia’s territorial integrity to satisfy Hitler’s apparently limited demand, buying time but losing the Czech army and fortifications.

items.stem: When did Italian forces invade Abyssinia?
items.answer: October 1935
items.markingKey: A. The invasion began on 3 October 1935; Addis Ababa fell in May 1936.

items.stem: Where did Chamberlain first meet Hitler during the Czech crisis of September 1938?
items.answer: Berchtesgaden
items.markingKey: A. The meetings were Berchtesgaden (15 Sept), Bad Godesberg (22 Sept) and Munich (29–30 Sept).

items.stem: A student claims that Hitler’s foreign policy aimed only to reverse the Treaty of Versailles. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Revision was a first stage, but Lebensraum in the East, as in Mein Kampf and the Hossbach Memorandum, went far beyond the 1914 borders; the occupation of Prague in March 1939 had nothing to do with Versailles.
items.markingKey: Revision was a first stage, but Lebensraum in the East, as in Mein Kampf and the Hossbach Memorandum, went far beyond the 1914 borders; the occupation of Prague in March 1939 had nothing to do with Versailles. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Pact of Steel (1939) and the Rome–Berlin Axis (1936).
items.answer: The Axis was an informal understanding of cooperation announced by Mussolini in November 1936; the Pact of Steel was a binding military alliance obliging each to support the other in any war.
items.markingKey: The Axis was an informal understanding of cooperation announced by Mussolini in November 1936; the Pact of Steel was a binding military alliance obliging each to support the other in any war. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Amara writes: "Germany invaded Poland in 1939 without any pretext." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The SS staged incidents such as the Gleiwitz radio station attack on 31 August 1939 to present Germany as the victim of Polish aggression.
items.markingKey: The SS staged incidents such as the Gleiwitz radio station attack on 31 August 1939 to present Germany as the victim of Polish aggression. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why Stalin signed the Nazi–Soviet Pact in August 1939.
items.answer: Stalin distrusted Britain and France after Munich, from which the USSR was excluded; Anglo-French negotiations in Moscow were slow and low-level; the pact bought time to rearm, avoided a two-front war with Japan (fighting at Khalkhin Gol) and offered territory in Poland and the Baltic.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Stalin distrusted Britain and France after Munich, from which the USSR was excluded; Anglo-French negotiations in Moscow were slow and low-level; the pact bought time to rearm, avoided a two-front war with Japan (fighting at Khalkhin Gol) and offered territory in Poland and the Baltic. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the structuralist interpretation and the intentionalist interpretation of Hitler’s foreign policy.
items.answer: Intentionalists (e.g. Trevor-Roper, Hildebrand) argue Hitler followed a long-held programme from Mein Kampf; structuralists/functionalists (e.g. Mommsen, Broszat) and A. J. P. Taylor stress opportunism, economic pressures and the dynamics of the Nazi state. Many historians combine fixed aims with opportunist methods.

items.stem:
Source C
Mussolini is worried. He has realised that Hitler is going to war and that Italy is bound to him by the Pact of Steel without having been consulted. The Duce feels that the moment is not right for us; we lack everything – raw materials, guns, aircraft. He alternates between the wish for honour, which pushes him towards Germany, and the knowledge of our unpreparedness.
— Count Galeazzo Ciano, Italian foreign minister, diary entry, August 1939 (paraphrased)

According to Source C, what can be learned about Italian entry into the Second World War? [3]
items.answer: Mussolini was anxious that Hitler would drag Italy into war without consultation; Italy lacked raw materials and weapons; Mussolini was torn between honour and awareness of unpreparedness.
items.markingKey: Mussolini was anxious that Hitler would drag Italy into war without consultation; Italy lacked raw materials and weapons; Mussolini was torn between honour and awareness of unpreparedness. items.stem:
Source D
[Photograph] Crowds of people in Vienna raise their arms in the Nazi salute and wave swastika flags as German troops in open vehicles drive along the Ringstrasse, March 1938.
— Description of a photograph published by the German news agency, 15 March 1938, during Hitler’s visit to Vienna after the Anschluss

What is the message conveyed by Source D? [2]
items.answer: The Anschluss appeared to be welcomed enthusiastically by Austrians; German troops were greeted as liberators rather than invaders.

items.stem:
Source D
[Cartoon] Hitler and Stalin bow to each other over the body of a dead soldier lying on the ground. Hitler says: “The scum of the earth, I believe?” Stalin replies: “The bloody assassin of the workers, I presume?”
— Description of the cartoon “Rendezvous” by David Low, Evening Standard, London, 20 September 1939

What is the message conveyed by Source D? [2]
items.answer: The Nazi–Soviet Pact was a cynical deal between bitter ideological enemies; their mutual hatred was hidden by politeness; the victim was Poland, crushed between them.

items.stem: Using the Corfu Incident (1923) as an example, explain early Fascist ambitions in foreign policy.
items.answer: After an Italian general was murdered on the Greek–Albanian border, Mussolini bombarded and occupied Corfu and withdrew only after Greece paid compensation, under pressure from the Conference of Ambassadors. It showed Mussolini’s desire for prestige through force and the willingness of the great powers to bypass the League, but also that in 1923 he still backed down under pressure.
items.markingKey: Context (After an Italian general was murdered on the Greek–Albanian border, Mussolini bombarded and occupied Corfu and withdrew only after Greece paid compensation, under pressure from the Conference of Ambassadors.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It showed Mussolini’s desire for prestige through force and the willingness of the great powers to bypass the League, but also that in 1923 he still backed down under pressure. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to early Fascist ambitions in foreign policy.

items.stem: A student claims that Italy entered the war in 1939 as Germany’s ally under the Pact of Steel. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Italy declared non-belligerence in September 1939 and entered the war only on 10 June 1940.
items.markingKey: Italy declared non-belligerence in September 1939 and entered the war only on 10 June 1940. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source D, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating German and Italian expansion, 1935–1939. [4]
items.answer: Value: It shows that many Austrians publicly welcomed union with Germany and how the regime publicised this support. Limitations: Released by the Nazi propaganda apparatus, it was selected to show enthusiasm; it omits opponents, Jews and those arrested in the first days, and cannot show how representative the crowd was.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that appeasement was a rational policy given Britain’s position in 1938?
items.answer: Given British constraints appeasement was understandable, but it rested on a misjudgement of Hitler’s aims.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: incomplete rearmament (radar and Spitfires not ready); Dominions and public opinion opposed war; threats from Japan and Italy to the empire; bought a year to rearm. Arguments against: Czechoslovakia’s 35 divisions and fortifications were lost; encouraged Hitler and alienated the USSR; German rearmament also advanced in 1938–39. Supported judgement: Given British constraints appeasement was understandable, but it rested on a misjudgement of Hitler’s aims. items.stem:
Source A
The acquisition of new soil for the settlement of our surplus population has an infinite number of advantages. But such a territorial policy cannot be carried out in the Cameroons; it can be carried out almost exclusively in Europe. If we speak of soil in Europe today, we can primarily have in mind only Russia and her vassal border states.
— Adolf Hitler, Mein Kampf, volume 2, written 1925–1926 (adapted translation)

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for an historian studying the causes of German and Italian expansion in the 1930s. [4]
items.answer: Value: Written by Hitler himself, it shows his ideological aims and the long-term goal of eastward expansion that historians link to his later policy. Limitations: It was written in prison in the mid-1920s to win followers, long before he held power; it is not a precise plan, and later policy was also shaped by opportunity and circumstance.

items.stem: Which country did Italy invade in April 1939?
items.answer: Albania
items.markingKey: D. Italy occupied Albania on 7 April 1939, a response to Hitler’s seizure of Prague.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Stresa Front"?
options: The Italian nationalist grievance (associated with D’Annunzio) that Italy had been denied the territory promised in the 1915 Treaty of London, such as Dalmatia and Fiume
The April 1935 agreement of Britain, France and Italy to resist German violations of Versailles, which collapsed over Abyssinia
The secret plan of December 1935 by the British and French foreign ministers to give Italy much of Abyssinia, abandoned after it was leaked
“living space”: Hitler’s aim, set out in Mein Kampf, of acquiring territory in Eastern Europe for German settlement at the expense of the Slavic peoples
items.answer: The April 1935 agreement of Britain, France and Italy to resist German violations of Versailles, which collapsed over Abyssinia
items.markingKey: B. "Stresa Front" is the April 1935 agreement of Britain, France and Italy to resist German violations of Versailles, which collapsed over Abyssinia.

items.stem: "Mussolini’s foreign policy was consistently aggressive from 1922." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: In the 1920s Mussolini mostly cooperated with Britain and France (Locarno 1925, Kellogg–Briand 1928) despite Corfu (1923); he even opposed Hitler over Austria in 1934 and joined the Stresa Front in 1935.

items.stem: Distinguish between the occupation of Prague in March 1939 and the remilitarisation of the Rhineland.
items.answer: The Rhineland was German territory and could be presented as revision of an unfair treaty; Prague was the seizure of non-German lands, which destroyed the argument that Hitler sought only self-determination for Germans and ended appeasement.

items.stem: Explain why Britain and France declared war on Germany in September 1939 but not in 1938.
items.answer: The occupation of Prague in March 1939 proved Hitler’s aims went beyond self-determination; Britain had given a guarantee to Poland; rearmament, especially radar and fighters, had progressed; public opinion had shifted, so a further concession was politically impossible.

items.stem: Using the Italian attack on the French Alps (June 1940) as an example, explain the opportunism and weakness of Italy’s entry into the war.
items.answer: Italy attacked France on 20 June, after the French government had already sought an armistice; the offensive made almost no progress before the armistice of 24 June. Mussolini sought gains cheaply at the last moment, but the failure revealed Italy’s military weakness and won him only a small occupation zone.

items.stem: A student claims that Hitler’s troops met strong resistance from the Austrian army in March 1938. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: There was no armed resistance: German troops were greeted by cheering crowds in many places and a plebiscite in April 1938 recorded 99 per cent approval, though under intimidation.
items.markingKey: There was no armed resistance: German troops were greeted by cheering crowds in many places and a plebiscite in April 1938 recorded 99 per cent approval, though under intimidation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Alessia writes: "The Nazi–Soviet Pact was a formal military alliance between Germany and the USSR." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It was a non-aggression pact with a secret protocol dividing spheres of influence, not a military alliance; it was broken by the German invasion of the USSR in June 1941.

items.stem:
Source A
Hitler’s foreign policy was that of his predecessors, of the professional diplomats at the foreign ministry, and indeed of virtually all Germans. He wished to free Germany from the restrictions of the peace treaty. In principle and doctrine, Hitler was no more wicked than many other contemporary statesmen.
— A. J. P. Taylor, British historian, The Origins of the Second World War (1961) (paraphrased)

According to Source A, what can be learned about the causes of German and Italian expansion in the 1930s? [3]
items.answer: Hitler’s aims were traditional German aims shared by diplomats and the public; he sought revision of Versailles; he was not uniquely wicked in principle.
items.markingKey: Hitler’s aims were traditional German aims shared by diplomats and the public; he sought revision of Versailles; he was not uniquely wicked in principle. items.stem: A student claims that Italy’s entry into the war greatly strengthened the Axis. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Italy’s armed forces performed poorly – in Greece, North Africa and at Taranto (November 1940) – and Germany had to divert forces to rescue its ally.
items.markingKey: Italy’s armed forces performed poorly – in Greece, North Africa and at Taranto (November 1940) – and Germany had to divert forces to rescue its ally. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the Abyssinian crisis was more damaging to the League of Nations than the Manchurian crisis.
items.answer: Abyssinia was more damaging because it exposed the failure of sanctions, the League’s main weapon, at the heart of the system.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: occurred in Europe’s sphere with League powers directly involved; sanctions were tried and failed openly; Hoare–Laval Pact revealed hypocrisy. Arguments against: Manchuria set the precedent of unpunished aggression; Japan’s withdrawal began the exodus of great powers; both together destroyed confidence. Supported judgement: Abyssinia was more damaging because it exposed the failure of sanctions, the League’s main weapon, at the heart of the system.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that the Treaty of Versailles was the most important cause of German expansion between 1933 and 1939?
items.answer: Versailles provided grievances and opportunities, but Nazi ideology explains the scale and direction of expansion.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: widespread resentment made revision popular (Rhineland, Saar, Sudetenland); military restrictions and territorial losses gave Hitler pretexts; weak successor states in Eastern Europe. Arguments against: Nazi ideology of Lebensraum and racial war went beyond revision; Prague (March 1939) and Poland were not justified by Versailles alone; appeasement and Soviet policy created opportunities. Supported judgement: Versailles provided grievances and opportunities, but Nazi ideology explains the scale and direction of expansion.
